results.title: Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects
results.content: # Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects. Power is sometimes also called “sensitivity.” Power refers to the ability of a test (i.e., an analysis of an experiment) to detect a “true effect” that is different from the null hypothesis (e.g., the ability to detect a difference between treatment and control when that difference actually exists). There are four factors that influence power: sample size, the true effect size, the variance of the effect, and the alpha-threshold (level of significance). If we have a more liberal threshold (i.e., a higher alpha level), we have more power to detect the effect. ## Power of a t-test. MDE tell us what is the smallest true effect, in standard deviations of the outcome, that is detectable for a given level of power and statistical significance. Because the standard deviation is influenced by sample size, MDE incorporates all of the information of a power calculation but does so in a way that applies to all experiments.

results.title: Power Analysis - Aris Paschalidis
results.content: The effect size can be interpreted as the “minimum clinically important difference.” In other words, the difference that an investigator wants to detect between study groups. If one were to compute the power using this observed effect size, the power would yield little additional information to the already known p-value. We can estimate various detectable effect sizes as we change the power. We define the effect size at a power of 0.8 as the *minimum detectable effect size* or MDES. Note that this is the same effect size that would have been used in an a priori power analysis. Given the observed p-value, observed effect size, the minimum detectable effect size, and the theoretical effect size of interest, we can make additional conclusions about our study. A comparison of the observed and minimum detectable effect size suggests whether a result is significant. If the observed effect size is greater than the minimum detectable effect size, it suggests that the results are significant. The larger the observed effect size, the larger the difference we found between the study cohorts. A comparison of the minimum detectable effect size and the theoretical effect size of interest indicates whether a study is over or underpowered. If the minimum detectable effect size is smaller than the theoretical effect size of interest, our study is appropriately powered. To think of this differently, if the minimum detectable effect size is greater than the theoretical effect size of interest, our study cannot ascertain differences that we consider to be theoretically or practically relevant, i.e., it is underpowered. However, it can be concluded that the study is adequately powered to detect effect sizes greater than the minimum detectable effect size. The study would then be adequately powered for effect sizes greater than 0.3 but would be unable to detect effect sizes less than 0.3. doi:10.7326/0003-4819-121-3-199408010-00008 On sample-size and power calculations for studies using confidence intervals. doi:10.1586/erp.11.9 Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863 doi:10.1525/collabra.33267 The 20% Statistician: Observed power, and what to do if your editor asks for post-hoc power analyses. doi:10.1080/17453674.2020.1755932 RPubs - Sample size estimation and Power analysis in R.

results.content: At its core, **sample size** refers to the number of individual data points or observations selected from a larger statistical population. Smaller effect sizes require larger sample sizes to achieve statistical significance. ## Sample Size Calculation: Formulas and Considerations. **Beyond Cochran’s Formula:** More complex study designs often require specialized sample size calculators or statistical software packages. * **Analysis of Variance (ANOVA):** The sample size should be large enough to ensure sufficient statistical power for detecting differences between group means. The smaller the effect you wish to reliably detect and the narrower the confidence interval required, the larger the sample size needed. * **Conduct a Pilot Study:** A small pilot study can help estimate the population variance and refine the sample size calculation. By understanding the principles of statistical power, effect size, and confidence intervals, and by utilizing appropriate sample size calculation methods, researchers and technologists can increase the validity and reliability of their findings, leading to more informed decisions and impactful innovations.
